explain.title: A function pairs inputs and outputs
explain.body: In y = f(x), x is the independent variable (input) and y is the dependent variable (output). A function can be shown as an equation, graph, table, or verbal description.

explain.title: Different functions have different graph shapes
explain.body: A linear function makes a straight line. A quadratic function makes a parabola: it opens upward when a > 0 and downward when a < 0. A cubic graph is a curve that can have at most two turning points.

explain.title: Reciprocal and exponential graphs
explain.body: A reciprocal function has the form y = a/x, with x ≠ 0. Its graph may approach asymptotes, which are lines that a graph approaches but never touches. An exponential function has the form y = kaˣ, where a > 1; y = 2ˣ is an increasing growth curve.

explain.title: Plot by making a table
explain.body: Choose several x-values, calculate y for each one, and plot the resulting points. Join the points with a straight line or a smooth curve that matches the type of function.

mistakes: Copying a sign incorrectly when substituting a negative x-value, especially when squaring or cubing.
Drawing a quadratic graph as a straight line instead of a parabola.
Joining plotted points with sharp corners instead of a smooth curve.
Forgetting that x cannot be zero in y = a/x, or plotting a point where a reciprocal function is undefined.
Drawing a reciprocal graph so that it touches an asymptote.
Leaving out labels, axes, intercepts, or the stated interval when sketching a graph.

explain.title: Exponential growth and decay
explain.body: In exponential growth, the graph starts slowly but accelerates rapidly as time progresses. In exponential decay, the graph starts high and decreases sharply before levelling off.

explain.title: Make a table before graphing
explain.body: Choose several values of time or another input, substitute them into the function, and record the outputs. Plot the ordered pairs and join them with a smooth curve when the relationship is exponential.

explain.title: Gradient at a point
explain.body: The gradient or slope of a graph at any point is equal to the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point. Remember that a tangent is a line that just touches a curve only at one point (and doesn’t cross it).

explain.title: Real-life graphs
explain.body: A straight salary graph can show the starting salary and yearly increase. For cost and revenue, the point where the graphs meet is the break-even point; revenue minus cost gives profit.

For profit, forgetting to subtract cost from revenue or forgetting the fixed-cost term in the function.
Giving a numerical answer without its units, such as bags, persons, years, or rupees.

explain.title: Straight-line graphs
explain.body: A linear function such as y = 5x + 3 has a straight-line graph. In y = mx + c, m is the slope and c is the y-intercept. The equation x = 5 gives a vertical line parallel to the y-axis.

explain.title: Quadratic graphs
explain.body: A function with x² has a parabola as its graph. If the coefficient of x² is positive, the parabola opens upward; if it is negative, it opens downward.

explain.title: Cubic graphs
explain.body: A function with x³ is cubic. To find where its graph meets the x-axis, set y = 0 and solve the resulting equation.

explain.title: Exponential graphs
explain.body: In an exponential function, the variable is in the exponent, as in y = 5^x. A base greater than 1 gives growth as x increases; a base between 0 and 1 gives decay.

explain.title: Reciprocal graphs and plotting
explain.body: In a reciprocal function such as y = 2/x, x cannot be zero. Make a table of input-output values, plot the points, and sketch the separate branches without joining them across x = 0.

explain.title: Using graphs in applications
explain.body: A graph can show how quantities such as sales, cost, revenue, supply, or demand change. The break-even point is where cost and revenue are equal, so it is the intersection of their graphs.

mistakes: Confusing the slope with the y-intercept in y = mx + c.
Thinking x = 5 is a horizontal line; it is vertical and parallel to the y-axis.
Choosing the wrong direction for a parabola by ignoring the sign of the coefficient of x².
Trying to calculate a reciprocal-function value at x = 0.
Plotting points inaccurately or joining the two branches of a reciprocal graph across the vertical axis.
Substituting the wrong value of t or leaving out the negative sign in the exponent when calculating sales.

notes.title: How to plot a function graph
notes.answer: A function graph shows the relationship between the input x and its output y.
notes.explanation: A function gives an output y for an input x. To graph a function, find several x-values, calculate the matching y-values, plot the points, and draw the appropriate line or curve.
notes.simple: Choose x-values, work out y, and plot the pairs (x, y). Join them with the right shape.
examples: For y = 3x − 5, x = 0 gives y = −5, so (0, −5) lies on the graph.
For y = x², x = −2 gives y = 4, so (−2, 4) lies on the graph.
steps: Substitute each x-value into the function to find y.
Write the ordered pairs (x, y) and plot them.
Join the points using the correct shape: a straight line, parabola, or smooth curve.
notes.checkQuestion: What shape is the graph of y = x², and which way does it open?
notes.checkAnswer: The graph is a parabola opening upward.

notes.title: Reading Growth, Decay and Real-Life Graphs
notes.answer: An exponential growth graph becomes steeper as time passes.
notes.explanation: Exponential graphs help us see how quantities change over time. For growth, the curve rises faster as time passes; for decay, it falls quickly at first and then levels off. For example, the village population model p = 753e^(0.03t) gives about 1016 people at t = 10. A tangent can also help estimate the gradient of a curve at one point.
notes.simple: Growth curves rise faster and faster; decay curves fall and then flatten. A tangent is used to estimate a curve’s gradient at one point.
examples: For p = 753e^(0.03t), the textbook estimates the population in 2020 (t = 10) as 1016 persons.
For the school-bag functions C(x) = 1200 + 20x and R(x) = 50x, the break-even quantity is 40 bags.
steps: Choose values of the independent variable, such as time t.
Substitute each value into the given function and make a table.
Plot the table values and join them with the appropriate curve or line.
Read estimates from the graph, or use the intersection of cost and revenue graphs to find a break-even point.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the steepness of an exponential growth graph as time passes?
notes.checkAnswer: The graph rises more steeply as time passes.

notes.title: Reading and sketching function graphs
notes.answer: Use the equation to find input-output pairs, then plot the pairs and draw the graph's shape.
notes.explanation: The graph of a function shows how its output y changes as its input x changes. To sketch a graph, choose values of the input, calculate the matching output, plot the points, and join them in the correct shape.
notes.simple: A graph is a picture of the pairs of input and output values that satisfy a function.
examples: For y = 5x + 3, the slope is 5 and the y-intercept is 3.
For y = 2/x, x cannot be 0 because division by zero is undefined.
steps: Identify the type of function from its equation.
Choose suitable values of the input and calculate the output for each.
Plot the ordered pairs on the axes.
Join the points with the appropriate shape: a line, curve, or two separate branches.
For a straight line, use the coefficient of x as the slope and the constant term as the y-intercept.
